overview:
In Jain philosophy, karma is not merely a metaphor for moral consequence but a subtle material substance (pudgala) that actually binds to the soul (jīva). This binding occurs through intentional activities of mind, speech, and body, and it obscures or conditions the innate qualities of the soul—its infinite knowledge, perception, bliss, and energy. The doctrine of karma subtypes (prakṛti-bheda) is therefore a technical map of how different karmic particles affect different aspects of spiritual and worldly existence.

Classically, Jain texts speak of eight principal types of karma (aṣṭa prakṛti), divided into two broad categories: ghātīyā (destructive or defiling) and aghātīyā (non‑destructive or non‑defiling). Ghātīyā karmas directly veil the essential attributes of the soul. These are: jñānāvaraṇīya (knowledge‑obscuring), darśanāvaraṇīya (perception‑obscuring), mohanīya (deluding), and antarāya (obstructing). Aghātīyā karmas do not touch the soul’s intrinsic purity but determine the external conditions of embodiment and experience: vedanīya (feeling‑producing), nāma (body‑determining), gotra (status‑determining), and āyu (lifespan‑determining). Together, these eight types structure the entire karmic architecture of saṃsāra.

Each of the eight principal types has further subtypes (upaprakṛti), which specify the exact mode in which karma operates. Tattvārthasūtra and its commentarial tradition commonly list 148 subtypes in total: 5 of jñānāvaraṇīya, 9 of darśanāvaraṇīya, 2 of vedanīya, 28 of mohanīya, 4 of āyu, 93 of nāma, 2 of gotra, and 5 of antarāya. These numbers may vary slightly between Digambara and Śvetāmbara exegetical traditions, but the underlying structure remains consistent. The subtypes are not arbitrary; they correspond to distinct spiritual functions—for example, different forms of knowledge, different modes of perception, different kinds of delusion, and different ways in which one’s body and social position are determined.

Jñānāvaraṇīya karma is said to obscure five forms of knowledge: sensory (mati), scriptural (śruta), clairvoyant (avadhi), telepathic (manaḥparyāya), and omniscient (kevala‑jñāna). Darśanāvaraṇīya karma similarly obstructs various modes of perception or intuition, such as ocular, non‑ocular, clairvoyant, and omniscient perception, with Śvetāmbara texts often expanding this into nine subtypes. Mohanīya karma, called the ‘king of karmas’, is divided into darśana‑mohanīya (delusion of right faith) and cāritra‑mohanīya (delusion of conduct), each with numerous sub‑categories that describe specific forms of attachment, aversion, and ethical confusion. Antarāya karma is classified into five subtypes that obstruct giving (dāna), gain (lābha), enjoyment (bhoga), re‑enjoyment or repeated enjoyment (upabhoga), and energy or capacity (vīrya).

On the aghātīyā side, vedanīya karma has two subtypes: śata‑vedanīya (pleasure‑producing) and aśata‑vedanīya (pain‑producing), which govern the felt tone of experience. Āyu karma is divided into four subtypes corresponding to the four main realms of rebirth—deva (heavenly beings), manuṣya (humans), tiryañca (animals and lower forms), and nāraka (hell‑beings)—and fixes the duration of life in each. Nāma karma, the most elaborately subdivided, has 93 (or slightly more in some lists) subtypes that determine the specific body type, species, form, color, structure, and other physical and psychological traits. Gotra karma has two subtypes—high status (uccagotra) and low status (nīcagotra)—which shape one’s family background and social standing.

From a practical standpoint, the doctrine of karma subtypes explains why beings differ so widely in knowledge, health, lifespan, social position, and spiritual receptivity. It also underpins the Jain path of purification: by understanding which karmas obscure which qualities, practitioners can apply appropriate disciplines of samvara (stoppage of new karmic influx) and nirjarā (shedding of accumulated karma). The complete destruction of the four ghātīyā karmas results in kevala‑jñāna (omniscience) while the soul is still embodied; the subsequent destruction of the four aghātīyā karmas at the end of that final life leads to mokṣa, the state of bodiless liberation. Although the technical lists of subtypes are intricate, their ethical message is clear: every intention and action shapes very specific aspects of one’s future experience, and liberation requires a precise, disciplined transformation of those karmic patterns.

Modern scholarship and traditional teachers alike emphasize that these subtypes should not be read as fatalistic categories. They are dynamic: karmas can be intensified, weakened, prematurely fructified, or transformed through one’s inner dispositions and practices. The detailed taxonomy of subtypes is therefore a sophisticated ethical and spiritual psychology, mapping how subtle variations in conduct and attitude crystallize into equally subtle variations in knowledge, perception, feeling, embodiment, and social context. For serious study, these lists are best approached alongside a qualified teacher and the primary texts, because translation choices and sectarian commentaries can differ on terminology and enumeration, even while agreeing on the core structure.

primary_sources.title: Tattvārthasūtra
primary_sources.author: Umāsvāti / Umāsvāmi
primary_sources.original_text: अद्य ज्ञानदर्शनावरण वेदनीय मोहनीय आयुष्क नाम गोत्रान्तरायाः।
primary_sources.translation: There are eight principal types of karmic bondage: knowledge‑obscuring, perception‑obscuring, feeling‑producing, deluding, lifespan‑determining, body‑determining, status‑determining, and obstructing.
primary_sources.notes: This sūtra (commonly cited as Tattvārthasūtra 8.5) is the foundational canonical statement listing the eight main karma types. Later verses and commentaries elaborate their subdivisions, functions, and the distinction between ghātīyā and aghātīyā karmas. Both Digambara and Śvetāmbara traditions accept this basic list, though they may differ slightly in the enumeration and naming of subtypes.

primary_sources.title: Tattvārthasūtra (subtype enumeration)
primary_sources.author: Umāsvāti / Umāsvāmi, with traditional commentaries
primary_sources.original_text: ज्ञानावरणस्य पञ्च, दर्शनावरणस्य नव, वेदनीयस्य द्वे, मोहनीयस्य अष्टाविंशतिः, आयुष्कस्य चत्वारि, नाम्नः त्रिणवत्यधिकं, गोत्रस्य द्वे, अन्तरायस्य पञ्च।
primary_sources.transliteration: jñānāvaraṇasya pañca, darśanāvaraṇasya nava, vedanīyasya dve, mohanīyasya aṣṭāviṃśatiḥ, āyuṣkasya catvāri, nāmnaḥ triṇavaty‑adhikaṃ, gotrasya dve, antarāyasya pañca
primary_sources.translation: There are five subtypes of knowledge‑obscuring karma, nine of perception‑obscuring, two of feeling‑producing, twenty‑eight of deluding, four of lifespan‑determining, ninety‑three of body‑determining, two of status‑determining, and five of obstructing karma.
primary_sources.notes: This verse is transmitted with minor textual variations across manuscripts and sectarian recensions, but it is widely cited in the commentarial tradition as giving the standard total of 148 karma subtypes. Detailed lists of each subtype are then provided in works such as Sarvārthasiddhi (Śvetāmbara) and Digambara commentaries, which explain the specific spiritual and experiential functions of each category.

primary_sources.title: Sarvārthasiddhi (commentary on Tattvārthasūtra)
primary_sources.author: Ācārya Pūjyapāda
primary_sources.original_text: मोहनीयः सर्वकर्मणां राजा, स हि सम्यग्दर्शनसम्यग्चरित्रयोः बाधकः। तस्य द्वे भेदे दर्शनमोहनीयं चरित्रमोहनीयं च, तयोः पुनरनेकविधा उपभेदाः।
primary_sources.transliteration: mohanīyaḥ sarva‑karmaṇāṃ rājā, sa hi samyag‑darśana‑samyag‑caritrayoḥ bādhakaḥ. tasya dve bhede darśana‑mohanīyaṃ caritra‑mohanīyaṃ ca, tayoḥ punar aneka‑vidhā upabhedāḥ.
primary_sources.translation: The deluding karma is the king of all karmas, for it obstructs right faith and right conduct. It has two main divisions: faith‑deluding and conduct‑deluding, and each of these in turn has many further sub‑divisions.
primary_sources.notes: Sarvārthasiddhi is a major Digambara commentary on Tattvārthasūtra. Here, Pūjyapāda explains the central role of mohanīya karma and introduces its subdivision into darśana‑mohanīya and cāritra‑mohanīya, which are then further analyzed into numerous upaprakṛtis. This passage illustrates how primary sūtra statements are expanded into detailed taxonomies of karma subtypes.

primary_sources.title: Gommaṭasāra Jīvakāṇḍa
primary_sources.author: Ācārya Nemicandra
primary_sources.translation: Karmas beginning with knowledge‑obscuring are ghātī (destructive) karmas, and those beginning with feeling‑producing are aghātī (non‑destructive) karmas.
primary_sources.notes: Gommaṭasāra Jīvakāṇḍa is a key Digambara text on the soul and karma. This succinct statement formalizes the division of the eight karma types into the two overarching categories of ghātīyā and aghātīyā, which is central to understanding how different karmas relate to the soul’s essential qualities versus its external conditions.

misconceptions.myth: The detailed subtypes of karma mean that everything in life is rigidly predetermined and cannot be changed.
misconceptions.reality: Jain doctrine holds that karmas are dynamic: their intensity, duration, and time of fruition can be altered through one’s mental states and practices such as samvara (stoppage) and nirjarā (shedding). The subtypes describe specific patterns of influence, but they do not remove agency; they show precisely how ethical and spiritual effort can transform future experience.

misconceptions.myth: Ghātīyā karmas are always more important than aghātīyā karmas, so physical and social conditions have no real spiritual significance.
misconceptions.reality: While ghātīyā karmas directly veil the soul’s intrinsic qualities and are crucial for liberation, aghātīyā karmas shape the bodily and social context in which spiritual practice occurs. Jain texts emphasize that unfavorable nāma, gotra, or āyu karmas can make practice harder, and favorable ones can support it. Both categories matter, though in different ways, and the path attends to all of them.

misconceptions.myth: The numbers of subtypes (such as 148) are fixed and identical across all Jain traditions and texts.
misconceptions.reality: The broad structure of eight main types and their division into ghātīyā and aghātīyā is shared, but specific counts and names of subtypes can vary slightly between Digambara and Śvetāmbara traditions and among different commentaries. Responsible study therefore compares editions and consults qualified teachers rather than assuming a single, universally fixed list.

misconceptions.myth: Karma subtypes are purely symbolic or psychological and do not involve any real ‘substance’.
misconceptions.reality: Classical Jain ontology treats karma as a form of subtle material pudgala that actually binds to the soul. Although modern interpreters sometimes use psychological language to explain the doctrine, primary texts consistently describe karma as a real, fine matter with specific modes (prakṛti) and quantities, not merely as metaphor or mental impression.
